newsitem.title: QATAR: Gulf Arabs, seeking unity, set for tense summit.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs, seeking unity, set for tense summit.

text.p: Gulf Arab states hold their annual summit this week in the heat of an espionage trial that threatens to destroy a carefully nurtured image of unity.

Despite many largely bilateral disputes, leaders of the six oil states on the Arab side of the Gulf have always temporarily put their differences aside to meet every year since they formed the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) in 1981.
But the dream of a strong political and economic alliance is more elusive than ever, and Bahrain, smallest and least wealthy of the six, has broken the unwritten rule of public unity.
"Look around you and you see that, no matter what, the Gulf (Arab) leaders meet every year," said a GCC analyst.

But Bahrain, locked in a territorial dispute with summit host Qatar which escalated with the arrest of two alleged Qatari spies who went on trial in Manama on Wednesday, has said it would not come to Doha for the summit due to open on Saturday.
Doha has denied that the arrested man and woman are spies.

And six years after Iraq invaded Kuwait, there are also differences on GCC policy towards Baghdad. A recently renewed call for reconciliation with Iraq by UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, the Gulf's elder statesman, has yet to find favour with his GCC partners.
Official sources and Western diplomats said even if Bahrain changed its mind and decided to attend its Emir Sheikh Isa bin Sulman al-Khalifa would stay away.
Neither King Fahd of Saudi Arabia, the GCC's dominant power, nor Sheikh Zaid is expected to attend for health reasons.

King Fahd, 75, suffered a stroke last year and has not left the kingdom for years. He sent Crown Prince Abdullah to the summit held in the Omani capital Muscat last December. Sheikh Zaid, 78, is still recovering from neck surgery in September.
Diplomats said the absence of King Fahd and Sheikh Zaid could influence Oman's Sultan Qaboos bin Said also to miss this gathering.
That would leave the Emir of Kuwait, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, as the only foreign head of state at the Doha summit.

Host Qatar was the first to disturb GCC unity a year ago when its new Emir, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, boycotted the summit's closing session in protest at the appointment of a Saudi national as GCC chief.
His delegation's highly public walkout -- transmitted live around the Gulf on television -- angered Sultan Qaboos and placed Doha on a collision course with its allies.

In the latest dispute, Bahrain wants Qatar, which controls the world's third largest natural gas reserves, to withdraw its claim to a cluster of reefs potentially rich in oil and gas from the International Court of Justice.
Qatar went to the court at The Hague in frustration at the GCC's inability to settle the dispute. Even mediation by GCC heavyweight Saudi Arabia has failed to find a solution.

The same dispute almost ruined the last summit in Doha in 1990 when Qatar insisted on raising the issue as huge U.S. transporters were landing at Doha airport with military hardware for the 1991 Gulf War to free Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.

Bahrain's absence and the expected poor showing by other GCC leaders this year "is not the end of the GCC...Most of this is personality differences," said a senior Western diplomat who predicted a return to closer coordination in the near future.

GCC leaders have been trying to form a common market, forge a security accord and integrate defences since the alliance's formation at the height of the Iran-Iraq war but no final agreements have been achieved.
